problemText: A data table adapted from the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects shows life expectancy at birth rising, between 1950 and 2019, as follows: World 46 to 73 years (a gain of about 27 years); Africa 37 to 62 years (a gain of about 25 years); Asia 42 to 74 years (a gain of about 32 years); Europe 62 to 79 years (a gain of about 17 years). Which region gained the MOST years of life expectancy over this period?
choices: Africa, whose 25-year gain, from a 1950 starting point of about 37 years, was the smallest gain of the three regions shown
Asia, rising from about 42 to about 74 years — a gain of about 32 years, the largest shown
Europe, whose already-high 1950 starting point of 62 years made its comparatively large 17-year gain possible without much difficulty
The world average, which by definition must reflect a larger overall gain than any single region taken alone
hints: Compare each region's ending figure to its own 1950 starting figure — subtract to find each region's gain, then compare the three gains directly.
Rule out any answer citing the world average or Europe — the world figure isn't a region, and Europe's 17-year gain is the smallest of the three shown, not the largest.

problemText: Between 1950 and 2019, Africa's life expectancy rose from about 37 to about 62 years (a gain of about 25 years), while Europe's rose from about 62 to about 79 years (a gain of about 17 years) — a SMALLER numerical gain than Africa's. Yet Europe's 2019 figure (79) remains well above Africa's (62). Which statement best explains this pattern?
choices: The life-expectancy figures reported for Africa must simply be unreliable or mismeasured for the year 1950
Europe's total population fell sharply after 1950, which mechanically raised its measured life expectancy figure
Africa's 25-year gain came entirely from one country, while Europe's 17-year gain was spread evenly across the region
A region's ranking reflects both its gain and its 1950 starting point, not the gain alone
hints: A region's 2019 ranking depends on where it started as well as how much it gained — check each region's STARTING figure before assuming the bigger gain must finish ahead.

Rule out any answer treating a smaller numerical gain as evidence of unreliable data or a shrinking population — Europe's higher finish reflects its much higher 1950 starting point, nothing more unusual.

problemText: A data table combining two ITU-tracked indicators shows worldwide mobile-cellular subscriptions rising from about 11 million in 1990 to about 738 million in 2000, about 5.29 billion in 2010, and about 8.26 billion in 2020. The same table's Internet-use row, using 2005 as its earliest year because no reliable single global aggregate exists before then, shows Internet use rising from 15.6% of the world's population in 2005 to 28.4% in 2010, 39.9% in 2015, and 60.1% in 2020. Mobile subscriptions passed one per person worldwide years before Internet use reached even half the world's population. This gap is best read as evidence for which pattern?
choices: "Leapfrogging" — many countries adopted mobile networks directly, without first building fixed telephone-line infrastructure, letting mobile technology spread faster
Mobile phones and Internet access spread at the same pace everywhere, differing only in which year each indicator's tracking began
Internet use could not have existed anywhere before 2005, since the earliest reliable global figure dates only to that year
Wealthier countries adopted mobile phones only after their fixed telephone-line networks had already reached full saturation
hints: Compare when each row's growth accelerates — mobile subscriptions already passed one-per-person by the mid-2010s, well before internet use reached even half the population — and think about what routes let mobile phones spread that fast.

Rule out any claim that the technologies spread at the same pace, or that the Internet didn't exist before 2005 — the table's 2005 start date reflects a gap in reliable global reporting, not the absence of earlier internet use.

problemText: A data table shows world container port throughput rising from about 36 million TEU in 1980 to about 792 million TEU in 2020 (roughly a 22-fold increase), while world merchandise exports in current (not inflation-adjusted) US dollars rose from about $1.97 trillion to about $17.73 trillion over the same span (roughly a 9-fold increase), with the dollar figure flattening somewhat after 2010 even as container volume kept climbing. Which indicator more reliably shows how much the PHYSICAL volume of world trade grew, and why?
choices: The dollar figure, because export value in current dollars directly counts the number of goods shipped, without any price distortion
Neither indicator is reliable, since both figures are limited to trade conducted in US dollars only
Container throughput, because it counts physical cargo units and is unaffected by the price and currency swings behind the dollar figure
The dollar figure, because its 9-fold increase is a larger absolute number of trillions than the container figure's 22-fold increase
hints: Ask which measure counts physical goods directly versus which measure mixes physical volume together with price and currency effects.

Rule out any answer favoring the dollar figure — a larger absolute number of trillions doesn't mean more physical goods moved, and both figures track worldwide trade, not only dollar-denominated trade.

problemText: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights' preamble states that "disregard and contempt for human rights have resulted in barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind," before proclaiming, in Article 1, that "all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights." Read together, these two clauses are best understood as responding to which immediate historical context?
choices: The overthrow of colonial governments across Asia and Africa, which the UDHR was written specifically to formalize
A binding wartime treaty among the Allied powers that the UDHR merely restated in different language
The founding of the United Nations in San Francisco in 1945, an event the preamble describes directly
The atrocities of World War II, which prompted the United Nations to proclaim this declaration
hints: Read the two clauses as cause and effect: what 'barbarous acts' had 'outraged the conscience of mankind' by 1948, prompting a universal declaration of equal dignity?

Rule out any answer describing a binding treaty or decolonization specifically — the preamble's language points to a very recent, global catastrophe, and the Declaration itself is a non-binding proclamation, not a treaty.

problemText: In his September 20, 2001 address to Congress, President Bush declared that the September 11 attacks meant "night fell on a different world, a world where freedom itself is under attack." Framing the attacks in this sweeping way — as an attack on "freedom itself," not only on the United States — served which purpose in the security-vs-rights debate this address opened?
choices: It limited the US response to a narrow law-enforcement investigation targeting only the individuals directly responsible for the attacks
It justified treating the response as a broad, sustained security effort, later paired with an explicit effort to distinguish terrorists from Muslims generally
It formally declared war against a specific named foreign government under existing constitutional procedures
It announced the immediate suspension of all diplomatic relations between the United States and every Muslim-majority country
hints: Notice that Bush frames the attack as being on 'freedom itself,' not just on the United States — think about what scale of response that broader framing supports.
Rule out any answer describing a narrow, individual-focused response or a formal declaration of war against a named government — neither matches the sweeping, open-ended framing of this line.

problemText: By the 2000s, capital, components, and finished goods were flowing among Asian, European, American, and other economies in complex, multidirectional supply chains — for example, China's post-1978 market reforms turned it into a major exporter TO the West, while the Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong) built export industries that reshaped global manufacturing from the 1960s onward. This pattern is best read as evidence against which claim about economic globalization after 1945?
choices: That the 1997 Asian financial crisis began with currency collapses in Thailand
That the World Trade Organization, established in 1995, replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
That globalization after 1945 mainly meant Western capital and goods flowing outward, one direction only
That the Bretton Woods conference of 1944 created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank
hints: Trace where capital and manufactured goods actually moved — into China and the Asian Tigers as well as out of them — before deciding whether 'flowing outward from the West' is an accurate one-line summary.
Rule out any answer restating an accurate but unrelated fact (the WTO's founding, Bretton Woods, or the 1997 crisis) — the question asks what the described pattern undermines, not what else is true.

problemText: The high-yield crop varieties of the Green Revolution (1940s-1960s) reached some regions and crops far more than others, and smallpox eradication — certified in 1980 — required the World Health Organization decades of sustained, coordinated vaccination campaigning even after an effective vaccine already existed. Together, these two examples are best read as evidence against which claim?
choices: That new technology spreads to every region at roughly the same pace and by the same route once it exists
That the Green Revolution increased crop yields across parts of Asia and Latin America from the 1940s through the 1960s
That smallpox was the first human disease ever eradicated worldwide through deliberate public-health action
That expanded irrigation and synthetic fertilizer use accompanied the high-yield crop varieties of the Green Revolution
hints: Ask whether the Green Revolution and smallpox eradication reached every place at the same time and by the same method, or unevenly and only after extended effort.
Rule out any answer restating an accurate but unrelated fact about the Green Revolution or smallpox eradication — the question asks which broader CLAIM the two examples undermine.

problemText: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) proclaims rights belonging to "all members of the human family." Which statement best describes the UDHR's legal status?
choices: it is a UN General Assembly declaration, not legally binding by itself, though foundational to later binding human-rights treaties
it is a binding treaty enforced by an international court with the power to overturn national laws
it is a military alliance requiring signatory states to defend each other's borders
it is a trade agreement establishing tariff rates among UN member states
hints: The UDHR proclaims a standard of rights but is not itself a binding legal instrument.
Rule out any answer describing a binding court-enforced treaty, a military alliance, or a trade agreement — none matches the UDHR's actual form.

problemText: Bollywood films from India, K-pop from South Korea, and football with roots spanning Europe, Latin America, Africa, and Asia all became widely popular across the globe after 1945. Which conclusion about cultural globalization is best supported by these three examples together?
choices: cultural globalization after 1945 was driven mainly by Hollywood and other American media and entertainment companies
global popular culture flowed outward from multiple centers, not along a single path from one dominant source
these three cultural forms stayed largely confined to their own countries or regions of origin throughout this period
football, Bollywood, and K-pop all originated in the same country before spreading worldwide
hints: Three different countries or regions of origin producing three genuinely global cultural phenomena is direct evidence against a single-source model of cultural globalization.
Rule out any answer crediting American media alone, claiming these forms stayed local, or claiming a shared origin — none matches the examples given.

problemText: The 1918 influenza pandemic, spread and worsened by the movement of troops during the final stages of World War I, killed an estimated tens of millions of people worldwide within about two years. Which factor most directly explains why this pandemic caused such a high death toll?
choices: it was deliberately spread as a biological weapon by one of the warring powers
it affected only elderly populations already suffering from other chronic illnesses
it struck before effective antiviral treatments or a vaccine existed, and spread rapidly through wartime troop movements
it stayed confined to a single country and did not spread across any international border
hints: No effective vaccine or antiviral treatment existed in 1918, and wartime troop movements accelerated the pandemic's spread.
Rule out any answer describing deliberate biological warfare, an elderly-only impact, or containment within one country — none matches the historical record.

problemText: The Montreal Protocol (1987), which phased out ozone-depleting chemicals, is widely regarded as a successful example of coordinated international environmental action, while the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015), aimed at reducing carbon emissions, have made comparatively slower and more contested progress. Which factor best explains this difference in international success?
choices: the Montreal Protocol addressed a problem scientists had already resolved decades before climate science reached any consensus
the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement were both fully implemented on schedule by every one of their signatory nations
no international environmental treaty had ever succeeded at anything before the Paris Agreement was finally signed in 2015
reducing carbon emissions carries greater economic stakes across the global fossil-fuel economy than phasing out ozone-depleting chemicals did
hints: Weigh the economic stakes of phasing out a narrower set of chemicals against the stakes of reducing fossil-fuel use across entire economies.

Rule out any answer claiming no scientific consensus existed for the Montreal Protocol, claiming complete Kyoto/Paris success, or denying any prior successful environmental treaty — none matches the historical record.

problemText: Representatives of the Allied powers met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire in 1944, before World War II had even ended, to create new international financial institutions. Which two institutions did this conference establish?
choices: the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank
the World Trade Organization and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
the United Nations and the League of Nations
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the Warsaw Pact
hints: Bretton Woods (1944) created institutions to stabilize currency exchange and fund postwar reconstruction, distinct from the trade-focused GATT/WTO created later.
Rule out the UN/League of Nations (political bodies) and NATO/Warsaw Pact (military alliances) — neither was created at Bretton Woods.

problemText: The 2008 global financial crisis began with a collapse in the US mortgage market but spread to banks and economies worldwide within months. Which broader point about the postwar global economy does this rapid spread best illustrate?
choices: the 2008 crisis stayed mostly confined to the United States, with only minor effects on any other country's economy
by 2008, national financial systems had grown so interconnected that a crisis in one major economy could no longer stay contained there
the International Monetary Fund had, by 2008, developed effective tools that eliminated the risk of any future crisis
the 2008 crisis originated simultaneously and independently in every major economy, with no single point of origin
hints: The crisis's rapid international spread from a single national origin point is the key evidence here.
Rule out any answer claiming the crisis stayed confined to the US, that the IMF had eliminated future crises, or that it had no single origin point — none matches the historical record.

problemText: From the 1940s through the 1960s, agricultural scientists developed high-yield, disease-resistant wheat and rice varieties, paired with expanded irrigation and synthetic fertilizer use. This set of agricultural innovations is known as —
choices: the Digital Revolution
the Bretton Woods System
the Green Revolution
the Non-Aligned Movement
hints: This agricultural transformation is specifically called the Green Revolution, distinct from later digital/communication changes.
Rule out the Digital Revolution (communication technology), Bretton Woods (financial institutions), and the Non-Aligned Movement (Cold War foreign policy) — none describes agricultural innovation.

problemText: An effective smallpox vaccine had existed for well over a century before the World Health Organization's campaign achieved the disease's global eradication, certified in 1980. Which statement best explains why eradication took so long after an effective vaccine already existed?
choices: the vaccine itself was not actually effective until the WHO's campaign began in the twentieth century
smallpox eradication was achieved instantly and simultaneously worldwide the moment the vaccine was first developed
the WHO's campaign focused mainly on wealthy countries, largely bypassing lower-income regions of the world
eradicating a disease worldwide required decades of sustained, coordinated global vaccination campaigning, not merely the existence of an effective vaccine
hints: An effective tool existing is different from the sustained global logistics needed to deploy it everywhere.

Rule out any answer claiming the vaccine was ineffective until the WHO campaign, claiming instant simultaneous eradication, or claiming the campaign ignored poorer countries — smallpox eradication specifically prioritized reaching the hardest, most under-resourced regions.

problemText: Beginning in the late 1970s, leaders such as Margaret Thatcher (UK), Ronald Reagan (US), and Deng Xiaoping (China) each moved their countries toward policies emphasizing free trade, deregulation, and reduced state control of the economy. Historians refer to this broad policy shift as —
choices: neoliberalism
mercantilism
détente
the Non-Aligned Movement
hints: Neoliberalism describes this late-twentieth-century turn toward free trade, deregulation, and privatization.
Rule out mercantilism (an early-modern doctrine), détente (a US-Soviet policy of eased tension), and the Non-Aligned Movement (a Cold War foreign-policy stance) — none describes this economic shift.

problemText: The World Trade Organization (WTO), established in 1995, replaced which earlier institution?
choices: the International Monetary Fund, created in 1944
the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, from 1947
the League of Nations, founded in 1920
the Non-Aligned Movement, founded in 1961
hints: GATT (1947) negotiated tariff reductions through successive rounds before being replaced by the permanent WTO in 1995.
Rule out the IMF (a separate institution created in 1944), the League of Nations (dissolved 1946), and the Non-Aligned Movement (a diplomatic stance, not a trade institution).

problemText: World trade as a share of global GDP was actually lower in the late 1940s than it had been in 1913, and did not recover to 1913 levels until the 1970s. This fact is best used as evidence against which claim about globalization?
choices: the claim that World War I had any effect on international trade patterns
the claim that the 1929 stock market crash occurred in the United States
the claim that globalization is an irreversible trend that never contracts once economies integrate
the claim that container shipping steadily reduced the cost of transporting goods internationally after 1970
hints: A multi-decade decline and slow recovery in trade's share of GDP is direct evidence that global economic integration can reverse, not just advance.
Rule out answers about WWI's effects, the 1929 crash's location, or container shipping's cost effects — none is the claim this specific fact refutes.

problemText: McDonald's restaurants in India sell menu items such as McAloo Tikki, adapted to local dietary practices and preferences, rather than an unmodified version of the chain's standard Western menu. This kind of local adaptation of a global product is best described by which concept?
choices: cultural homogenization, in which local cultures are steadily replaced by one unmodified global culture
protectionism, a trade policy restricting the import of any foreign goods or brands
neocolonialism, a critique of continued economic dependency on former colonial powers
glocalization, the adaptation of global products and ideas to local cultural contexts
hints: The India-specific menu adaptation is a case of a global brand blending with local preferences, not replacing them wholesale.

Rule out cultural homogenization (implies no local adaptation at all), protectionism (a trade-restriction policy), and neocolonialism (an economic-dependency critique) — none matches this specific pattern of local product adaptation.
